tier_reason: The README of the ACM TOMS 2018 paper's companion repo (sharase/melg-64, by Harase and Kimoto, not the SFMT authors) has a table of CPU seconds for 1e9 64-bit outputs: SFMT19937-64 with SIMD 1.8457 s vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s (Core i7-3770) and 2.8806 s vs 6.6490 s (Phenom II X6 1045T), gcc -O3. That is a peer-reviewed third-party measurement, but the timing harness is not in the repo (only generator directories) and the gcc version is not given, so not A.

corrections.caveats: Numbers come from a third-party table in the melg-64 README (companion repo of Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 44(3) 2018), measured on 2012-era CPUs with an unstated gcc version; the melg-64 repo holds only the MELG generators, not the timing harness for SFMT or MT19937-64. The baseline is the original mt19937-64.c, not libstdc++ std::mt19937_64. The SFMT README itself has no numbers, and the authors' homepage claim ('about twice as fast as MT') could not be opened (egress blocked). The SIMD path computes the same generator as the scalar one: the repo's check.sh diffs the std, sse2, avx2 and altivec test builds against the same reference outputs (SFMT.<MEXP>.out.txt). Quality trade-off noted on the same page: for 64-bit output SFMT19937 has a large equidistribution defect (Delta 14095 vs 7820 for MT19937-64), since SFMT is tuned for 32-bit output; dSFMT is the recommended variant for doubles. SFMT also produces a different sequence than MT19937, so it is a replacement generator, not a faster std::mt19937.

notes: Numbers verified verbatim on the melg-64 README; derived ratios (2.8x Intel, 2.3x AMD) are correct. Repo metadata confirmed via the github.com page: BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE.txt), 96 stars, not archived, last commit 2021-05-18 (abandoned).

tier_reason: First-party Quick Bench bar charts in the README (benchmarks/results/*.png) compare the engines against std::mt19937, std::default_random_engine, std::minstd_rand, rand() and std::uniform_int_distribution; benchmark code is public (benchmarks/engine_comparison.cpp, random_bounded_integer.cpp, random_bounded_float.cpp) but compiler, flags, standard library and CPU are not stated (the Quick Bench links are not reachable here), so C.

corrections.caveats: Numbers exist only as Quick Bench bar charts (ratio CPU time / no-op time) with no hardware, compiler, flags or standard library stated; values were read by eye from the PNGs and match the record (raw next(): std::mt19937 about 13,300 vs RomuDuoJr about 2,700, QuarkBurst64 about 2,600). The raw-engine chart compares 64-bit-output engines against the 32-bit-output std::mt19937 per call (std::mt19937_64 appears only in the bounded-integer chart, about 15,800). The harness sums outputs and calls DoNotOptimize only once after the loop. The fastest engines are ports of third-party generators (Romu, quarkburst/GhostScramble, konadare192px++, xoshiro256**, PCG32), so the entry mainly curates and packages third-party winners; third-party engine headers keep their own licenses (public domain, Apache-2.0, MIT). The upstream eightomic/quarkburst page returned 404 in the search run, and the RNG Battle Royale (2020) page was not opened. The C rand() % bound baseline is biased and only a performance reference, as the benchmarks README says. 1 star, single author.

notes: Chart values and README text match the record. Metadata confirmed on github.com: MIT, 1 star, 232 commits, last commit 2026-08-20 (active). quick-bench.com is egress-blocked, so compiler settings stay unknown.

tier_reason: The README (generated from README.Rmd) shows first-party bench::mark medians against R's rnorm and sample.int with no hardware, compiler or flags; no C++-level comparison against std::mt19937 was found in the README or the dqrng vignette, so C.

corrections.caveats: The baseline is R's built-in RNG and sampling functions, not std::mt19937 or another C++ generator; no C++ benchmark against std:: engines exists in the README or vignettes/dqrng.Rmd. No hardware or compiler is stated. The speedups mix a different engine with different algorithms (Ziggurat normals vs R's inversion; different sampling algorithms), so they are not generator-only gains, and the 63x sampling-without-replacement figure is largely algorithmic. Licensing: dqrng's own code is AGPL-3 (strong copyleft with a network clause), while the vendored generator headers are permissive (inst/include/pcg_* Apache-2.0 or MIT, inst/include/xoshiro.h CC0) per LICENSE.note; the bundled C++ headers depend on Rcpp/BH/sitmo for the R-facing parts.

notes: All three README numbers and the derived ratios (7.6x, 24x, 63x) check out. Metadata confirmed: DESCRIPTION License AGPL-3, 50 stars, not archived, last commit 2025-06-29 (stale).
